claim: Central neurons mediating vestibulo-spinal reflexes and self-motion perception optimally encode natural self-motion.
source: We have previously reported that central neurons mediating vestibulo-spinal reflexes and self-motion perception optimally encode natural self-motion (Mitchell et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mitchell et al., 2018.

claim: The vestibular nuclei comprise neuronal classes that mediate the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) and its adaptation.
source: Importantly however, the vestibular nuclei also comprise other neuronal classes that mediate essential functions such as the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) and its adaptation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about vestibular nuclei organization.

claim: Neurons displaying lower variability faithfully represented the stimulus' detailed time course.
source: Specifically, neurons displaying lower variability did not whiten naturalistic self-motion but instead faithfully represented the stimulus' detailed time course, while neurons displaying higher variability displayed temporal whitening.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing differences in coding strategies based on variability.

claim: Neurons displaying higher variability displayed temporal whitening.
source: Specifically, neurons displaying lower variability did not whiten naturalistic self-motion but instead faithfully represented the stimulus' detailed time course, while neurons displaying higher variability displayed temporal whitening.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing temporal whitening in high variability neurons.

claim: Faithful stimulus encoding is necessary to generate the compensatory eye movements found experimentally during naturalistic self-motion.
source: Using a well-established model of VOR pathways, we demonstrate that faithful stimulus encoding is necessary to generate the compensatory eye movements found experimentally during naturalistic self-motion.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Heterogeneities in resting discharge variability mediate a trade-off between faithful encoding and optimal coding via temporal whitening.
source: Here we show that heterogeneities in resting discharge variability mediate a trade-off between faithful encoding and optimal coding via temporal whitening.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: VO neurons mediate vestibulo-spinal reflexes as well as self-motion perception.
source: Specifically, we focused on a class of neurons within the vestibular nuclei, vestibular-only (VO) neurons, that mediate vestibulo-spinal reflexes as well as self-motion perception (Abzug et al., 1974; Shinoda et al., 1988; Gdowski and McCrea, 1999; Meng et al., 2007; Marlinski and McCrea, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: VO neurons optimally encoded naturalistic self-motion stimuli through temporal whitening.
source: Our results revealed that VO neurons optimally encoded naturalistic self-motion stimuli through temporal whitening (i.e., the spike train power spectrum is independent of temporal frequency and thus "white") because both neuronal variability and tuning were matched to effectively complement natural stimulus statistics (Carriot et al., 2014; Carriot et al., 2017; Mitchell et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PVP neurons make the primary contribution to the VOR.
source: Specifically, position-vestibular-pause (PVP) neurons make the primary contribution to the VOR, whereas eye-head (EH) neurons receive cerebellar input and are required for VOR adaptation and motor learning (see Cullen, 2012 for review) (Lisberger, 1984; Lisberger, 1994; Lisberger et al., 1994; Ramachandran and Lisberger, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: EH neurons receive cerebellar input and are required for VOR adaptation and motor learning.
source: Specifically, position-vestibular-pause (PVP) neurons make the primary contribution to the VOR, whereas eye-head (EH) neurons receive cerebellar input and are required for VOR adaptation and motor learning (see Cullen, 2012 for review) (Lisberger, 1984; Lisberger, 1994; Lisberger et al., 1994; Ramachandran and Lisberger, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The VOR generates robust compensatory eye movements in response to head movements encountered during everyday life in order to stabilize gaze.
source: The VOR generates robust compensatory eye movements in response to head movements encountered during everyday life in order to stabilize gaze (Goldberg et al., 2012) and is an attractive model for understanding how information transmitted by sensory neurons is actually decoded downstream to generate behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Goldberg et al., 2012.

claim: The VOR requires that information as to the detailed timecourse of head movements be contained in the spiking activities of sensory neurons and transmitted to motor areas.
source: Importantly, the VOR requires that information as to the detailed timecourse of head movements be contained in the spiking activities of sensory neurons and transmitted to motor areas.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement based on understanding of VOR function.

claim: All three neural classes (PVP, EH, and VO) displayed a similar wide range of variability as quantified by the coefficient of variation (CV) of the resting discharge.
source: We first establish that, in the absence of stimulation, all three neural classes displayed a similar wide range of variability as quantified by the coefficient of variation (CV) of the resting discharge.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neurons displaying high resting discharge variability displayed temporal whitening.
source: We found that, within each class, neurons displaying high resting discharge variability displayed temporal whitening.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Neurons displaying lower resting discharge variability did not display temporal whitening but instead faithfully encoded the stimulus's detailed timecourse.
source: In contrast, neurons displaying lower resting discharge variability did not display temporal whitening but instead faithfully encoded the stimulus's detailed timecourse as assessed by linear stimulus reconstruction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using linear stimulus reconstruction.

claim: Faithful encoding was greatest for PVP neurons.
source: Interestingly, our results show that faithful encoding was greatest for PVP neurons, suggesting that this coding strategy is necessary to generate the compensatory VOR eye movements observed during naturalistic self-motion stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing coding fractions across neuron types.

claim: Single-unit recordings were made from PVP (N = 20), EH (N = 15), and VO (N = 17) neurons within the vestibular nuclei of macaque monkeys.
source: In order to investigate the effects of differences in variability on coding strategy for naturalistic self-motion by central vestibular neurons, single-unit recordings were made from PVP (N = 20), EH (N = 15), and VO (N = 17) neurons within the vestibular nuclei of macaque monkeys (Figure 1A, top).
evidence: This describes the experimental dataset collected.

claim: PVP, EH, and VO neurons were identified using standard methodology that characterized a given neuron's responses to rotational vestibular stimulation in the yaw axis and eye movements.
source: PVP, EH, and VO neurons were identified using standard methodology (reviewed in Cullen, 2012) that characterized a given neuron's responses to rotational vestibular stimulation in the yaw axis (1 Hz, 40°/s peak velocity) and eye movements (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the methodology used for neuron classification, supported by citation.

claim: The vestibular and eye movement sensitivities of PVP, EH, and VO neurons in the dataset agreed with previously published values.
source: The vestibular and eye movement sensitivities of PVP, EH, and VO neurons in our dataset are shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and agreed with previously published values (Roy and Cullen, 2002; Roy and Cullen, 2003; Massot et al., 2011; Mitchell et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with cited prior work and data shown in figures.

claim: PVP and EH neurons can be distinguished based on their differential sensitivities to eye and head movements during smooth pursuit and VOR cancellation.
source: In particular, we note that PVP and EH neurons can be distinguished based on their differential sensitivities to eye and head movements during smooth pursuit and VOR cancellation, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Trial-to-trial variability in the neural response to repeated presentations of a given stimulus is largely determined by the variability of the resting discharge for vestibular neurons.
source: Such trial-to-trial variability is largely determined by the variability of the resting discharge for vestibular neurons (Sadeghi et al., 2007; Massot et al., 2011; Jamali et al., 2013; Mitchell et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Central vestibular neurons displayed resting discharges that were quite variable (PVP: 58 ± 19 sp/s, CV = 0.26 ± 0.13; EH: 47 ± 19 sp/s, CV = 0.40 ± 0.17; VO: 50 ± 18 sp/s, CV = 0.35 ± 0.18).
source: Our results show that central vestibular neurons displayed resting discharges that were quite variable (PVP: 58 ± 19 sp/s, CV = 0.26 ± 0.13; EH: 47 ± 19 sp/s, CV = 0.40 ± 0.17; VO: 50 ± 18 sp/s, CV = 0.35 ± 0.18).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of resting discharge properties.

claim: For neurons with low variability, the spike train power spectrum varied strongly as a function of frequency.
source: Indeed, for neurons with low variability, the spike train power spectrum varied strongly as a function of frequency.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Spectral power displayed local maxima at the neuron's firing frequency (i.e., the fundamental) as well as higher harmonics (i.e., integer multiples of the fundamental) for neurons with low variability.
source: Notably, spectral power displayed local maxima at the neuron's firing frequency (i.e., the fundamental; Figure 1B) as well as higher harmonics (i.e., integer multiples of the fundamental).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Spectral power was low within the frequency range of natural self-motion (i.e., 0–20 Hz) for neurons with low variability, which is expected as theory predicts spectral power at low frequencies is proportional to CV².
source: Spectral power was low within the frequency range of natural self-motion (i.e., 0–20 Hz; see orange bands in bottom panels of Figure 1B), which is expected as theory predicts spectral power at low frequencies is proportional to CV2 (Holden, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and theoretical prediction from Holden, 1976.

claim: The spike train power spectrum of more irregular neurons was more independent of frequency as evidenced from lack of local maxima at higher harmonics.
source: In contrast, the spike train power spectrum of more irregular neurons was more independent of frequency as evidenced from lack of local maxima at higher harmonics (Figure 1B, top panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The CV distribution was unimodal for all neuron classes.
source: It is important to note that the CV distribution was unimodal for all neuron classes (Figure 1C, bottom) which suggests that variability is distributed along a continuum for central neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Variability is distributed along a continuum for central neurons.
source: It is important to note that the CV distribution was unimodal for all neuron classes (Figure 1C, bottom) which suggests that variability is distributed along a continuum for central neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the unimodal distribution of CV values.

claim: The mean firing rate was not significantly correlated with CV for all central vestibular neuronal classes (PVP: R = −0.08, p=0.71; EH: R = −0.29, p=0.29; VO: R = −0.38, p=0.13).
source: We found that the mean firing rate was not significantly correlated with CV for all central vestibular neuronal classes (PVP: R = −0.08, p=0.71; EH: R = −0.29, p=0.29; VO: R = −0.38, p=0.13).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There were no significant differences between the resting firing rates of PVP, EH, and VO neurons (p≥0.11, one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni correction).
source: Further, we did not observe any significant differences between the resting firing rates of PVP, EH, and VO neurons (p≥0.11, one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni correction; Figure 1D, top panel) in general, except that PVP neurons displayed significantly lower CV values than EH neurons (p<0.03, one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni correction; Figure 1D, bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: PVP neurons displayed significantly lower CV values than EH neurons (p<0.03, one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni correction).
source: Further, we did not observe any significant differences between the resting firing rates of PVP, EH, and VO neurons (p≥0.11, one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni correction; Figure 1D, top panel) in general, except that PVP neurons displayed significantly lower CV values than EH neurons (p<0.03, one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni correction; Figure 1D, bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The power spectra of PVP, EH, and VO neurons displaying high variability were independent of frequency.
source: Our analysis revealed that the power spectra of PVP, EH, and VO neurons displaying high variability were independent of frequency (Figure 2D, solid curves) as they did not deviate from the Poisson confidence interval with the exception of low (<1 Hz) frequencies for the example EH neuron (Figure 2D, gray bands).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Spectral power for PVP, EH, and VO neurons displaying low variability decayed similarly to the stimulus power spectrum with increasing frequency and was thus not independent of frequency.
source: In contrast, spectral power for PVP, EH, and VO neurons displaying low variability decayed similarly to the stimulus power spectrum with increasing frequency and was thus not independent of frequency (Figure 2D, compare dashed curves to solid black).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The whitening index similarly depended on CV for all neuronal classes.
source: Overall, we found that the whitening index similarly depended on CV for all neuronal classes (Figure 2E, left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The whitening index was independent of resting discharge firing rate.
source: Further, we found that the whitening index was independent of resting discharge firing rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and the whitening index computed from neurons whose resting discharge firing rates were within a narrow range (45–55 sp/s) strongly depended on CV (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The whitening index computed from neurons whose resting discharge firing rates were within a narrow range (45–55 sp/s) strongly depended on CV.
source: Further, we found that the whitening index was independent of resting discharge firing rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and the whitening index computed from neurons whose resting discharge firing rates were within a narrow range (45–55 sp/s) strongly depended on CV (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Neural sensitivity was independent of variability.
source: These results, together with the fact that neural sensitivity was independent of variability (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggest that the differences in whitening are primarily due to differences in variability and, as such, are universal for central vestibular neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The differences in whitening are primarily due to differences in variability and are universal for central vestibular neurons.
source: These results, together with the fact that neural sensitivity was independent of variability (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggest that the differences in whitening are primarily due to differences in variability and, as such, are universal for central vestibular neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the independence of whitening from firing rate and sensitivity, but dependence on CV.

claim: A simple model in which changes in variability were explored systematically correctly fits data from PVP, EH, and VO neurons across all levels of resting discharge variability.
source: Overall, this model correctly fits data from PVP, EH, and VO neurons across all levels of resting discharge variability (Figure 2E, left panel, red curve).
evidence: This claim is supported by model predictions matching experimental data.

claim: A linear-nonlinear cascade model that included the effects of variability accurately predicted the response power spectra of individual neurons.
source: Overall, this model accurately predicted the response power spectra of the same six example neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by model predictions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: There was excellent agreement between predicted and actual whitening index values for the dataset (Student's t-test, PVP: F(19) = 0.44, p=0.66; EH: F(14) = 0.98, p=0.34; VO = F(16)=0.96, p=0.35).
source: As such, there was excellent agreement between predicted and actual whitening index values for our dataset (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C; Student's t-test, PVP: F(19) = 0.44, p=0.66; EH: F(14) = 0.98, p=0.34; VO = F(16)=0.96, p=0.35).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of model predictions with experimental data.

claim: The power spectrum of the resting discharge variability was not different from that of the trial-to-trial variability during stimulation for the dataset.
source: We note that the power spectrum of the resting discharge variability was not different from that of the trial-to-trial variability during stimulation for our dataset (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: On average, whitening index values for PVP and EH neurons were comparable to those obtained for VO neurons.
source: On average, whitening index values for PVP and EH neurons were comparable to those obtained for VO neurons (Figure 2E, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Central neurons with lower variability displayed lower noise power than their counterparts with higher variability.
source: Overall, central neurons with lower variability as quantified by the CV of the resting discharge displayed lower noise power than their counterparts with higher variability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) decreased with increasing variability.
source: As such, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) decreased with increasing variability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: Central vestibular neurons with lower variability transmit more information than those with higher variability.
source: This latter result is important as it suggests that central vestibular neurons with lower variability actually transmit more information than those with higher variability.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher SNR observed in low variability neurons.

claim: The mutual information rate decreased significantly with increasing CV.
source: To test this, we computed the mutual information rate (see Materials and methods) for our dataset and found a significant decrease with increasing CV, thereby confirming our hypothesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: Optimality of coding (i.e., the mutual information divided by its maximum possible value for a given level of variability) increased significantly with increasing CV.
source: Finally, we quantified optimality of coding (i.e., the mutual information divided by its maximum possible value for a given level of variability) and found a significant increase with increasing CV (Figure 2—figure supplement 7), thereby confirming results obtained using the whitening index.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: While central vestibular neurons with high variability transmit less information in absolute terms than their counterparts with low variability, they are more optimal in the sense that the mutual information is closer to the maximum possible value.
source: Thus, while central vestibular neurons with high variability transmit less information in absolute terms than their counterparts with low variability, they are more optimal in the sense that the mutual information is closer to the maximum possible value.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results on mutual information and optimality of coding.

claim: There was a strong negative correlation between CF (coding fraction) and variability as quantified by CV (All data: R = −0.53, p=10−4; PVP: R = −0.51; p=0.02; EH: R = −0.07, p=0.8; VO: R = −0.65,p=4.5×10−3).
source: Overall, we found a strong negative correlation between CF and variability as quantified by CV (Figure 3C; All data: R = −0.53, p=10−4; PVP: R = −0.51; p=0.02; EH: R = −0.07, p=0.8; VO: R = −0.65,p=4.5×10−3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: CF was independent of the resting discharge firing rate (All data: R = 0.13, p=0.34; PVP: R = 0.05, p=0.82; EH: R = 0.01, p=0.96; VO: R = −0.06, p=0.81).
source: Further, we found that CF was independent of the resting discharge firing rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A: All data: R = 0.13, p=0.34; PVP: R = 0.05, p=0.82; EH: R = 0.01, p=0.96; VO: R = −0.06, p=0.81).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: CF computed from neurons whose firing rates were within a narrow range (45–55 sp/s) strongly depended on CV (All data: R = −0.54, p=0.03; PVP: R = −0.96, p=0.03; EH: R = −0.20, p=0.7; VO: R = −0.87, p=0.02).
source: Moreover, CF computed from neurons whose firing rates were within a narrow range (45–55 sp/s) also strongly depended on CV (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B: All data: R = −0.54, p=0.03; PVP: R = −0.96, p=0.03; EH: R = −0.20, p=0.7; VO: R = −0.87, p=0.02).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Changes in CF were primarily due to changes in the resting discharge CV.
source: These results strongly suggest that changes in CF were primarily due to changes in the resting discharge CV.
evidence: This is inferred from the independence of CF from firing rate but dependence on CV.

claim: There was no significant correlation between neural sensitivity and variability.
source: This is because, as mentioned above, there was no significant correlation between neural sensitivity and variability (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PVP neurons displayed the largest coding fraction, followed by VO neurons, and EH neurons displayed the lowest coding fractions overall.
source: Overall, PVP neurons displayed the largest coding fraction, followed by VO neurons, and EH neurons displayed the lowest coding fractions overall (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Neurons with low variability more faithfully represented the stimulus' detailed time course in their spiking activities than their counterparts with high variability.
source: These results demonstrate that neurons with low variability more faithfully represented the stimulus' detailed time course in their spiking activities than their counterparts with high variability.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher coding fractions observed in low variability neurons.

claim: Variability establishes a trade-off between faithful stimulus encoding and temporal whitening.
source: Thus, together with our results above showing that neurons with low variability do not display temporal whitening, we conclude that variability establishes a trade-off between faithful stimulus encoding and temporal whitening.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results on temporal whitening and faithful encoding.

claim: Both animals generated robust compensatory eye movements characterized by gains approaching unity during naturalistic self-motion stimulation.
source: We found that indeed both animals generated robust compensatory eye movements characterized by gains approaching unity, such that the eye velocity was essentially the opposite of head velocity (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was much better agreement between the predicted and actual eye velocity signals when the input from a PVP neuron with low variability was used compared to high variability.
source: We found that there was much better agreement between the predicted and actual eye velocity signals when the input from an example PVP neuron with low variability was used (compare right and left panels in Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by model predictions shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was a strong negative correlation between the matching index and variability (R = −0.64, p=2.4×10−3 for PVP neurons).
source: There was a strong negative correlation between the matching index and variability (R = −0.64, p=2.4×10−3; Figure 4D, magenta), suggesting that PVP neurons with lower variability that faithfully represent the detailed time course of head movements make the primary contribution to generate compensatory VOR eye movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of model predictions.

claim: PVP neurons with lower variability that faithfully represent the detailed time course of head movements make the primary contribution to generate compensatory VOR eye movements.
source: There was a strong negative correlation between the matching index and variability (R = −0.64, p=2.4×10−3; Figure 4D, magenta), suggesting that PVP neurons with lower variability that faithfully represent the detailed time course of head movements make the primary contribution to generate compensatory VOR eye movements.
evidence: This is inferred from the negative correlation between matching index and variability.

claim: The performance of neuron pairs with low variability was overall greater than that obtained when considering pairs with low and high variability.
source: Overall, we found that the performance of neuron pairs with low variability was overall greater than that obtained when considering pairs with low and high variability (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), which confirms our proposal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Results for EH neurons were qualitatively similar to those obtained for PVP neurons regarding VOR generation (R = −0.64, p=0.01).
source: Overall, results for EH neurons were qualitatively similar to those obtained for PVP neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Figure 4D, blue; R = −0.64, p=0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Figure 4D.

claim: The activities of VOR neurons with low variability are best matched to the known dynamics of downstream decoders in order to generate compensatory VOR eye movements.
source: Thus, taken together, our results point to an important functional role for VOR neurons with low variability that faithfully represent the detailed time course of head movements. Specifically, the activities of these neurons are best matched to the known dynamics of downstream decoders in order to generate compensatory VOR eye movements.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results showing better match between predicted and actual eye movements for low variability neurons.

claim: Heterogeneities in resting discharge variability within each class strongly influenced coding strategies.
source: Overall, we found that heterogeneities in resting discharge variability within each class strongly influenced coding strategies.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Neurons with lower resting discharge variability transmitted the highest amounts of information and thus most faithfully encoded the stimulus' detailed timecourse.
source: Specifically, neurons with lower resting discharge variability transmitted the highest amounts of information and thus most faithfully encoded the stimulus' detailed timecourse.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by experimental data on mutual information and coding fraction.

claim: Neurons with higher resting discharge variability most optimally encoded the stimulus via temporal whitening, as their mutual information rates were closer to the maximum possible value.
source: In contrast, neurons with higher resting discharge variability most optimally encoded the stimulus via temporal whitening, as their mutual information rates were closer to the maximum possible value.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by experimental data on optimality of coding.

claim: PVP neurons, on average, more faithfully encoded the stimulus' detailed time course as compared to the two other classes, as quantified by their higher coding fraction values.
source: Interestingly, we found that PVP neurons, on average, more faithfully encoded the stimulus' detailed time course as compared to the two other classes, as quantified by their higher coding fraction values.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by experimental data on coding fractions.

claim: Faithful stimulus encoding, rather than temporal whitening, is required to generate the compensatory VOR eye movements measured during naturalistic self-motion stimulation.
source: Using well-established models of VOR pathways, we showed that faithful stimulus encoding, rather than temporal whitening, is required to generate the compensatory VOR eye movements measured in our experiments during naturalistic self-motion stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by modeling results.

claim: The detailed time course of head motion can be best recovered from the spiking activities of PVP neurons during naturalistic stimulation.
source: Here we show for the first time that the detailed time course of head motion can be best recovered from the spiking activities of PVP neurons during naturalistic stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by experimental data on stimulus reconstruction.

claim: The properties of the oculomotor plant effectively make it a low-pass filter.
source: Because the properties of the oculomotor plant effectively make it a low-pass filter, the relationship between extraocular motoneuron activity and eye movement must have compensatory frequency dependent dynamics (reviewed in Robinson, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Robinson, 1981.

claim: The properties of extraocular motoneurons complement those of the oculomotor plant during the VOR.
source: More recent studies have shown that the properties of extraocular motoneurons indeed complement those of the oculomotor plant (reviewed in Cullen, 2012) during the VOR (Sylvestre and Cullen, 1999; Ramachandran and Lisberger, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PVP neurons receive afferent input from the periphery and project directly to extraocular motoneurons to generate compensatory VOR eye movements within 5 ms.
source: Because PVP neurons receive afferent input from the periphery and in turn project directly to extraocular motoneurons to generate compensatory VOR eye movements within 5 ms (Huterer and Cullen, 2002), information must be decoded with little or no integration time as achieved by a coding strategy based on faithful stimulus encoding.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Huterer and Cullen, 2002.

claim: Information must be decoded with little or no integration time as achieved by a coding strategy based on faithful stimulus encoding for PVP neurons.
source: Because PVP neurons receive afferent input from the periphery and in turn project directly to extraocular motoneurons to generate compensatory VOR eye movements within 5 ms (Huterer and Cullen, 2002), information must be decoded with little or no integration time as achieved by a coding strategy based on faithful stimulus encoding.
evidence: This is inferred from the short latency of VOR pathways.

claim: Temporal whitening requires filtering of the input and thus more complex decoding strategies with larger integration times.
source: In contrast, we argue that temporal whitening, which requires filtering of the input and thus more complex decoding strategies with larger integration times, are not suitable for feedforward control of direct VOR pathways.
evidence: This is based on theoretical understanding of temporal whitening.

claim: Temporal whitening is not suitable for feedforward control of direct VOR pathways.
source: In contrast, we argue that temporal whitening, which requires filtering of the input and thus more complex decoding strategies with larger integration times, are not suitable for feedforward control of direct VOR pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for fast decoding in VOR pathways.

claim: The VOR shows remarkable linearity in that the resulting eye movements effectively compensate for head movements over a wide range of frequencies and amplitudes.
source: Specifically, the VOR shows remarkable linearity in that the resulting eye movements effectively compensate for head movements over a wide range of frequencies and amplitudes (Huterer and Cullen, 2002; Ramachandran and Lisberger, 2006; Sadeghi et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PVP neurons demonstrate substantial nonlinearities: their spiking activity is silenced for off-direction rotations and demonstrates saturation for on-direction rotations for velocities greater than 200 °/s.
source: In contrast, PVP neurons demonstrate substantial nonlinearities: their spiking activity is silenced for off-direction rotations and demonstrates saturation for on-direction rotations for velocities greater than 200 °/s (Roy and Cullen, 2004; Ramachandran and Lisberger, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Extraocular motoneurons display substantial nonlinearities.
source: In this context, it is important to note that previous studies have shown that extraocular motoneurons display substantial nonlinearities (Sylvestre and Cullen, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sylvestre and Cullen, 1999.

claim: For higher amplitude stimuli, PVP neurons that perform temporal whitening may contribute to compensating the nonlinear properties of extraocular motoneurons to ensure a robust VOR.
source: It is further conceivable that, for higher amplitude stimuli than the ones considered in the present study, PVP neurons that perform temporal whitening contribute to compensating the nonlinear properties of extraocular motoneurons to ensure a robust VOR.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential roles of high variability PVP neurons.

claim: EH neurons least faithfully followed the naturalistic stimulus' detailed time course as compared to other central vestibular neuronal classes.
source: Specifically, EH neurons least faithfully followed the naturalistic stimulus' detailed time course as compared to other central vestibular neuronal classes (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: EH neurons displayed weak sensitivities to artificial vestibular sinusoidal stimuli and are more strongly driven by pursuit signals.
source: This result is consistent with previous observations that EH neurons displayed weak sensitivities to artificial vestibular sinusoidal stimuli and are more strongly driven by pursuit signals (Roy and Cullen, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roy and Cullen, 2003.

claim: EH neurons responded to naturalistic head motion such that their spiking activities were temporally whitened.
source: Our results show that EH neurons responded to naturalistic head motion such that their spiking activities were temporally whitened.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The larger integration time windows needed to properly decode information transmitted via temporal whitening by EH neurons may be beneficial for VOR adaptation and motor learning.
source: We hypothesize that the larger integration time windows needed to properly decode information transmitted via temporal whitening by EH neurons are beneficial for VOR adaptation and motor learning.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: VO neurons project to the thalamus as well as to the spinal cord.
source: These functions are mediated by a distinct class of neurons within the vestibular nuclei (i.e., VO neurons) that project to the thalamus (Meng et al., 2007; Marlinski and McCrea, 2009) as well as to the spinal cord (Abzug et al., 1974; Shinoda et al., 1988; Gdowski and McCrea, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The majority of VO neurons displayed high variability and optimally encoded naturalistic head motion stimuli via temporal whitening.
source: Specifically, our new findings reveal that, while the majority of VO neurons displayed high variability and optimally encoded naturalistic head motion stimuli via temporal whitening, a minority of VO neurons displayed low variability and instead faithfully followed the stimulus' detailed time course.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A minority of VO neurons displayed low variability and instead faithfully followed the stimulus' detailed time course.
source: Specifically, our new findings reveal that, while the majority of VO neurons displayed high variability and optimally encoded naturalistic head motion stimuli via temporal whitening, a minority of VO neurons displayed low variability and instead faithfully followed the stimulus' detailed time course.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Temporal whitening by VO neurons with high variability is functionally advantageous for the control of vestibulo-spinal reflexes.
source: We speculate that temporal whitening by VO neurons with high variability is functionally advantageous for the control of vestibulo-spinal reflexes.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning by the authors.

claim: The response dynamics of irregular versus regular afferents are best matched to the mechanical demands of the vestibulo-spinal reflex versus the VOR, respectively.
source: Further, the response dynamics of irregular versus regular afferents are best matched to the mechanical demands of the vestibulo-spinal reflex versus the VOR, respectively (Fernandez and Goldberg, 1971; Bilotto et al., 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fernandez and Goldberg, 1971 and Bilotto et al., 1982.

claim: Irregular but not regular afferents display spike timing precision/phase locking.
source: Recent studies have further shown that irregular but not regular afferents display spike timing precision/phase locking (Jamali et al., 2016; Jamali et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jamali et al., 2016 and Jamali et al., 2019.

claim: Spike timing precision/phase locking was also observed at the next level (central neurons).
source: Interestingly, spike timing precision/phase locking was also observed at the next level (Jamali et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jamali et al., 2016.

claim: Spike timing precision/phase locking induces greater synchrony at the VO population level that in turn better compensates for the inertia of the head-neck system.
source: We hypothesize that this single neuron property induces greater synchrony at the VO population level that in turn better compensates for the inertia of the head-neck system (reviewed in Cullen, 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, with a citation to Cullen, 2019.

claim: Temporal whitening by VO neurons with high variability that preferentially receive input from irregular afferents provides enhanced information at the population level.
source: As such, we propose that temporal whitening by VO neurons with high variability that preferentially receive input from irregular afferents provides enhanced information at the population level, as seen in other systems (Doi et al., 2012; Kastner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a proposal by the authors, with citations to Doi et al., 2012 and Kastner et al., 2015.

claim: VO neurons project to the thalamus and are thought to play a role in self-motion perception and spatial orientation computation.
source: To answer this question, it is useful to consider that VO neurons also project to the thalamus and thus are thought to play a role in self-motion perception and spatial orientation computation (Meng et al., 2007; Marlinski and McCrea, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Meng et al., 2007 and Marlinski and McCrea, 2009.

claim: The subset of VO neurons that faithfully follows the stimulus' detailed timecourse may preferentially project to thalamus in order to provide information as to the detailed timecourse of head movements.
source: One possibility is that the subset of VO neurons that faithfully follows the stimulus' detailed timecourse preferentially projects to thalamus in order to provide information as to the detailed timecourse of head movements.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning by the authors.

claim: Temporal whitening gives rise to maximal information if the input SNR is high.
source: Theoretical studies have shown that temporal whitening gives rise to maximal information if the input SNR is high (van Hateren, 1992a; Rieke et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to van Hateren, 1992a and Rieke et al., 1996.

claim: When the input noise for a given frequency is high (i.e., a low input SNR), optimal coding is achieved by filtering out the neural output at that frequency due to noise contamination.
source: In the case where the input noise for a given frequency is high (i.e., a low input SNR), optimal coding is instead achieved by filtering out the neural output at that frequency due to noise contamination (van Hateren, 1992a), which has been observed in the retina for weak stimulus intensities (van Hateren, 1992b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to van Hateren, 1992a and van Hateren, 1992b.

claim: Both regular and irregular vestibular afferents that provide input to central neurons display low trial-to-trial variability during naturalistic self-motion stimulation.
source: However, this is unlikely to be the case here since both regular and irregular vestibular afferents that provide input to central neurons display low trial-to-trial variability during naturalistic self-motion stimulation (Sadeghi et al., 2007; Jamali et al., 2016; Mitchell et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sadeghi et al., 2007, Jamali et al., 2016, and Mitchell et al., 2018.

claim: The input SNR to central vestibular neurons is very likely to be high, such that optimized coding is achieved via temporal whitening according to theory.
source: As such, the input SNRto central vestibular neurons is very likely to be high, such that optimized coding is achieved via temporal whitening according to theory.
evidence: This is inferred from the low trial-to-trial variability of afferent inputs.

claim: Central neurons within VOR pathways receive input primarily from regular afferents which display the least trial-to-trial variability during stimulation and thus the highest input SNR.
source: Moreover, as mentioned above, central neurons within VOR pathways receive input primarily from regular afferents (Goldberg et al., 1987; Sato and Sasaki, 1993) which display the least trial-to-trial variability during stimulation and thus the highest input SNR (Sadeghi et al., 2007; Jamali et al., 2016; Mitchell et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Variability is distributed along a continuum for all central neural classes, which is different than for vestibular afferents in which variability displays a bimodal distribution with two distinct classes: regular and irregular.
source: Notably, our results show that variability is distributed along a continuum for all central neural classes. This is different than for vestibular afferents in which variability displays a bimodal distribution with two distinct classes: regular and irregular (Goldberg, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Goldberg, 2000.

claim: Differences in variability across central neurons may be due to different amounts of feedforward input from regular and irregular afferents.
source: Thus, one possibility is that differences in variability across central neurons are due to different amounts of feedforward input from regular and irregular afferents.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning by the authors.

claim: Differences in the intrinsic properties of central neurons may contribute to differences in variability.
source: Another possibility, which is not mutually exclusive, is that differences in the intrinsic properties of central neurons contribute to differences in variability (Babalian and Vidal, 2000; Ris et al., 2001; Sekirnjak and du Lac, 2002; Kodama et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning by the authors, with citations to prior work.

claim: Central vestibular neurons receive direct input from central structures including cortical, cerebellar, as well as numerous brain stem nuclei.
source: Finally, it is important to note that central vestibular neurons also receive direct input from central structures including cortical, cerebellar, as well as numerous brain stem nuclei (Akbarian et al., 1994; Voogd et al., 1996; McCrea and Horn, 2006) (see (Angelaki and Cullen, 2008) for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Central inputs likely contribute to shaping neuronal variability.
source: These central inputs also likely contribute to shaping neuronal variability.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning by the authors.

claim: Extracellular recordings in the cerebellar flocculus reveal irregularities in the spontaneous simple spike firing rate of Purkinje cells, which provides a clear source of variability to EH neurons.
source: For example, extracellular recordings in the cerebellar flocculus reveal irregularities in the spontaneous simple spike firing rate of Purkinje cells (Hoebeek et al., 2005), which provides a clear source of variability to EH neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hoebeek et al., 2005.

claim: All experimental protocols were approved by the McGill University Animal Care Committee and complied with the guidelines of the Canadian Council on Animal Care.
source: All experimental protocols were approved by the McGill University Animal Care Committee and complied with the guidelines of the Canadian Council on Animal Care.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Two rhesus macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta) were prepared for chronic extracellular recording using aseptic surgical techniques.
source: Two rhesus macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta) were prepared for chronic extracellular recording using aseptic surgical techniques as previously described (Mitchell et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects and methods.
